on 8 June 2023 by the Dirección General del Territorio Marítimo y de Marina Mercante

(DIRECTEMAR). The circular establishes mandatory cybersecurity and information-security

requirements for port facilities as part of maritime cyber risk management. It requires

ports to implement a structured cyber risk management system aligned with international

standards and to integrate this system into security assessments and port protection

plans under the ISPS Code. Ports must identify and mitigate cyber risks affecting critical

systems—such as access control, communications, cargo handling systems, and other

operational technologies—designate a responsible cybersecurity officer, and report

cyber incidents to the competent maritime authority. Compliance is verified through a

combination of internal and external audits, and strategically significant port

facilities are required to incorporate cyber risk management into their overall

security studies and general security plans.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience

10

Box 3 Cybersecurity considerations within the ISPS Code

The ISPS Code is structured in two parts:

• Part A sets out mandatory requirements, including the obligation for port facilities to

conduct a Port Facility Security Assessment and to develop, implement, and maintain

an approved Port Facility Security Plan. The latter defines measures to prevent, detect,

and respond to security threats affecting port infrastructure, operations, personnel,

and cargo.

• Part B provides non-mandatory guidance on how to meet the requirements of Part A,

including illustrative examples of risks and mitigation measures.

Despite its broad governance scope, the ISPS Code was designed primarily to address

physical security risks and has undergone only limited updates since its adoption.

Cybersecurity is not included among the mandatory requirements in Part A. References

2. Practice: Develop and maintain an up-to-date inventory of physical and IT assets and identify

critical assets needed for the continuous operation of the port ecosystem. Continuously

assess cyber risk exposure, implement risk mitigation measures and business continuity plans,

and clearly define responsibilities. These plans should be validated with internal or external

tests and exercise drills, and resources should be focused on the most critical systems, key

providers, and sensitive data, to maintain or rapidly recover port operations. Modernize legacy

technologies, leverage advanced technologies such as AI-based tools to enhance resilience,

and assess emerging technologies for cyber risks early in the adoption lifecycle. Organizations

are encouraged to move from a reactive, incident-driven approach to cybersecurity toward a

proactive, continuous management system.

Effective cyber risk management favors a continuous, proactive approach. This means anticipating

threats, improving controls, monitoring digital signals, and making changes on a continuous basis,

rather than waiting to react after incidents occur, as illustrated in Figure 6 below. This shift reduces

cyber exposure and incident response time by embedding prevention, detection, and response into daily

operations, whereas a reactive model largely focuses on post-incident containment and recovery.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience

35

2.3 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

Many ports struggle to maintain a current risk picture and implement security controls into

routine operations across IT/OT. At the same time, incident readiness remains under-practiced and

insufficiently integrated with business continuity. A central challenge of cybersecurity in ports is

the transition from one-off risk-gauging efforts to continuous outcomes-focused risk management

(IMO 2025). By integrating cybersecurity responsibilities into established processes, such as risk

management, operations oversight, business continuity planning, and procurement, ports can

strengthen resilience without creating parallel institutional frameworks.

Recommendation 1: Conduct an asset inventory

Ports should identify the key systems and processes within the port by defining the perimeter

results.source: Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf
results.text:
relevant to the organization and conducting a comprehensive asset inventory. Conducting an asset

inventory also helps the organization identify critical components necessary for business continuity.

This should include IT and OT assets, and document all connections, whether intended or legacy,

between the environments.

Recommendation 2: Conduct regular risk assessments

Risk assessments should be conducted at planned intervals and when significant changes to port

systems occur. In practice, this likely means conducting a comprehensive assessment annually, with

risk-based or trigger-based reassessments.

Recommendation 3: Implement practical risk mitigation measures

System protection is a core element of cybersecurity risk management. Even relatively simple

measures, such as clearly defining acceptable user behavior for online accounts or mandatory

refresh cycles for software and physical infrastructure housing IT systems, can significantly improve

2.2.4 Integrating Cybersecurity into Day-to-Day

Business Operations

It is possible to make cybersecurity a core requirement for new system procurement, from planning

and budgeting to specifications, deployment, and operations. This helps embed continuous, proactive

cyber risk management practices into contracts. Concession agreements in ports can mandate

minimum cybersecurity standards, for example through (World Bank 2025c):

• information-sharing obligations,

• periodic cybersecurity exercises,

• alignment with international guidelines or standards,

• requiring access controls for users,

• monitoring of systems,

• clear update and vulnerability patch processes, and other measures.

3.2 Financial Barriers

Even where ports recognize the skills gap discussed above, they frequently cannot justify

the investment — not because they are indifferent to risk, but because the financial logic of

cybersecurity works against them. Among World Bank survey respondents, funding cybersecurity

is an important barrier for more than 50 percent of ports across all income groups. The lack of a

business case is also widely recognized as a core barrier among ports. Unlike the human capacity

barriers discussed above, financial barriers concern what ports are willing to spend. This is distinct

from the market failures discussed in Section 3.3, which persist even where the financial case

becomes clear and adequate investments are present.

Security in general and cybersecurity in particular do not provide direct revenue to an organization

results.source: Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf
results.text:
accompanied by broad awareness programs for ports workforce. Financial barriers include funding

pressures and the perceived absence of a compelling business case. These factors reduce investment

in cybersecurity controls, as such measures avert losses rather than produce measurable revenue.

Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:

if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called

negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without

contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make

it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers

to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial

barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).

3.1 Human Capacity Barriers

results.source: Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf
results.text:
Port leadership buy-in remains a key bottleneck, with more than 50 percent of surveyed ports

citing funding constraints and many lacking a compelling internal business case for cybersecurity

investment. To address this, ports should translate cyber risks into financial terms by linking

investments to potential losses avoided, using available frameworks and tools. Where incident cost

estimation is highly uncertain, operational metrics—such as detection and response times—can

complement financial analysis by providing concrete, decision-relevant indicators of cybersecurity

performance. Establishing this internal business case is a necessary foundation for sustained and

prioritized cybersecurity spending.

ensuring functioning international trade and, therefore, global prosperity. The digitalization of port

infrastructure and operations will see fundamental growth over the next few decades. As such,

cyber risks are likely to grow at a similar pace, and port stakeholders are well advised to recognize

and anticipate such risks. Ports face a triple lock of barriers: they lack the people to manage

cyber risk, the financial incentives to prioritize it, and the market structures that would reward

collective action. These barriers are mutually reinforcing, and addressing any one of them in isolation

is insufficient.

Human capacity barriers include skills mismatches and the need for effective, specialized training,

3.2 Financial Barriers

Even where ports recognize the skills gap discussed above, they frequently cannot justify

the investment — not because they are indifferent to risk, but because the financial logic of

cybersecurity works against them. Among World Bank survey respondents, funding cybersecurity

is an important barrier for more than 50 percent of ports across all income groups. The lack of a

business case is also widely recognized as a core barrier among ports. Unlike the human capacity

barriers discussed above, financial barriers concern what ports are willing to spend. This is distinct

from the market failures discussed in Section 3.3, which persist even where the financial case

becomes clear and adequate investments are present.

Security in general and cybersecurity in particular do not provide direct revenue to an organization

[world-bank-cybersecurity-ports-2026:54:para:1 | Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf | page 54]
accompanied by broad awareness programs for ports workforce. Financial barriers include funding

pressures and the perceived absence of a compelling business case. These factors reduce investment

in cybersecurity controls, as such measures avert losses rather than produce measurable revenue.

Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:

if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called

negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without

contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make

it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers

to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial

barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).

3.1 Human Capacity Barriers

[world-bank-cybersecurity-ports-2026:69:para:3 | Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf | page 69]
Port leadership buy-in remains a key bottleneck, with more than 50 percent of surveyed ports

citing funding constraints and many lacking a compelling internal business case for cybersecurity

investment. To address this, ports should translate cyber risks into financial terms by linking

investments to potential losses avoided, using available frameworks and tools. Where incident cost

estimation is highly uncertain, operational metrics—such as detection and response times—can

complement financial analysis by providing concrete, decision-relevant indicators of cybersecurity

performance. Establishing this internal business case is a necessary foundation for sustained and

prioritized cybersecurity spending.
